build: Software Projects disk, alternate D64 with LA–LJ files

exclude: Disk staging for bytes copied to $1E00 and graphics decoded to $4000; disk tail remains in the queue.
extra: Scene bytes copied by the runtime loader
Tail of the file loaded at $8010, role unresolved

comments.text: The first copied byte in the scene record is $07. The caller starts executing one byte later.

Save and reload the caller stack pointer, install raster target $2BFD at line $FA and select multicolour bitmap mode in the bank at $4000. Initialize board state and choose a value for $2DFA from $24.
Reload the saved stack, select raster line $FA and set bitmap mode with the bitmap at $4000 and matrix at $7C00. Clear the board-related state bytes and choose the initial $2DFA value from $24.
Sample the joystick, wait two CIA2 periods and call the board update routines. If the player is idle, use fire to start the path that sets $2DCC and requests sound $87.
Clear the move timer $2D7E, set the busy flag $2D04 to $FF from zero, queue sound $83 and set $2D7F to 1.
Update the board move and its timer. Return with a nonzero outcome after the thresholds on $2E72 and $2D7E are met while $2EB0 is set.

Increment the animation step at $2D7E. Below 13, choose the movement path from the saved direction. At the limit clear the pose flag, install the standing pose and use $2D80 to decide whether to enter the restart sequence.
Subtract the indexed vertical displacement and $2D7F from Dirk's low Y. Apply the corresponding coordinate update and include two horizontal steps when the displacement flag is set.

On the first animation step, apply the upper row bound, increment the saved board row and check the destination. When the destination check returns $FF, undo the row increment and clear the extra displacement flag.
On the first animation step, check the zero-column bound before decrementing the saved column. Restore the old column and clear the extra displacement flag if the destination check returns $FF.
Subtract the target column and row from the saved player column and row. Continue only when each difference is zero, one or minus one.

Skip the check during a movement pose. Compare the saved player cell with pairs in the recorded cell history beginning at $2E8F. A match calls the resident cue and changes the colours of the player sprite group.
Use the selected board column at $2EA9 to form a vertical offset with stride 12 and a horizontal offset with stride 24. Combine these with the board-origin values and the selected row.
Return $FF for the current selected cell. Otherwise multiply the player row by ten, add the column and read that entry from the cell-type table.
Index the board table by the selected column and ten times the selected row, then save the type to $2EA1.
Check the active board flags and timer. On timer expiry select a random nibble below nine for one coordinate and begin computing the other coordinate.
Copy 128 bytes from $6200 to $6D00 before joining the common animation setup at $2324.
Copy 128 bytes of sprite shapes from $6280 into $6D00. Convert the selected board cell to sprite coordinates and position the first part of its effect 12 pixels to the right.
Install frame pointers $B4 and $B5 for sprites 6 and 7, set their colours to 5 and enable them. Request sound $81 and advance both Y positions during the timed loop.
Set sprites 6 and 7 to colour 5 while $2EAF counts down, or colour 0 when it is zero. If bit 0 of $2E6F is set, disable those sprites and reset the effect state.
Test the controller enable and the divider. At expiry reload the divider from $2E6E, advance the secondary countdown and select the next target movement path from the activity state.
Decrement the directional movement budget. Use $2E68 to choose one of four changes to the target column or row. Test the resulting cell and restore the old coordinate when the board check rejects it.
Decrement the movement delay, then choose an axis using the random generator at $173D. Compare the player and target board coordinates to select a direction on that axis.
Use two calls to the random generator to set $2E68 to a two-bit value and $2E71 to a three-bit value with bits 0 and 1 set.
Reload the movement delay with five and use the selected target column and row to calculate sprite and board addresses. Synchronize to the raster before installing the effect.
Shift the sequences beginning at $2E74 and $2E8F by two and add the newest pointer pair and two position bytes at their heads.
Return after the board update. The sprite strip compositor starts at the following byte.
Mask the saved cell pointer to a ten-bit offset, multiply by eight and add bitmap base $4000. Use the result to address the pixel rows for the board effect.
Read successive source bytes through $2A, recolour each byte at $2705, and write through $2C with Y and X descending.
Visit each two-bit pixel in A. Replace colours 1 and 2 with the corresponding pair from $2EA2. Preserve colours 0 and 3 and return the recoloured byte in A.
Add $0140, the width of one bitmap character row in bytes, to the source pointer at $2A.
Convert the target's low Y after offset $2B to a row and multiply it by 40. Subtract $18 from low X with the saved high X bit to form the column input, then derive the screen address for the target.
Multiply the target row at $2E64 by ten, add the column at $2E63, and save the cell type read from $2DFE at $2EA1.

Perform 20 delayed passes over 128 bytes beginning at $6D00, masking each byte with CIA1 timer A low. Set the colours of sprites 6 and 7 to white before the passes and disable those sprites afterward.
For sprite 5 Y below $41, set its colour to 6. Otherwise advance its colour, request sound $8A and decrement Y when the counter at $2EB2 expires.
Initialize 18 entries beginning at $2E74 to zero and 18 entries beginning at $2E8F to $FF.
Select a six- or seven-step animation limit based on the chosen direction. Increment the pose step and clear the movement flag once it reaches the limit.

Use the direction to select one of two frame-pair families and a mirror flag. Install the selected frames in sprites 0 and 4, copy two indexed displacement bytes and call the coordinate updater at $2991.
Use the second frame-pair and displacement tables, with the mirror flag set, before applying the coordinate update.

Choose the $C0 frame quartet for directions 0 and 3 or $A8 for directions 1 and 2. Mirror the shapes for directions 1 and 3. Stage the four pointers at $2DCE, then order them into the primary sprite slots.
Copy the player's high X bit to the companion sprite before applying the signed offsets from $2DCA and $2DCB. Correct the high bit when the low coordinate crosses the byte boundary.
A second RTS byte, immediately after the return from the companion sprite coordinate update.
Refresh the joystick. When a move can begin, check up, down, right and left in that order and store direction 0, 1, 2 or 3 in $2D05.
Set the movement flag, toggle the frame group and initialize two step fields. Test the active-low joystick bits and set the matching board direction before returning.
Use direction 0–3 to select one of the two four-pointer groups and its mirror flag. Transform the frames with the resident routine and store them into the board matrix sprite pointer table.
Add the step at $2D6F to the shared low X coordinate of sprites 0–3. Set their four high-X bits if the addition carries. Preserve A.
Subtract the step at $2D6F from the shared low X coordinate of sprites 0–3. Clear their four high-X bits if the subtraction borrows. Preserve A.
Copy sprite 0 X to sprites 1–3, align sprite 1 to its Y and place sprites 2 and 3 21 pixels lower before applying colours.
Set sprites 0 and 2 to colour 2 and sprites 1 and 3 to colour 7.
Keep sprites 1 and 2 on the original sprite 0 row and move sprites 0 and 3 21 pixels down. Set sprites 1 and 3 to colour 2 and sprites 0, 2 and 4 to colour 7.
Copy sprite 1 Y to sprite 0 and set sprites 2 and 3 21 pixels lower. Set colours for sprites 1 and 3 before the tail call that applies the four standard colours.
Choose the second quartet for values 4 through 12 at $2D7E, or the first quartet otherwise. Set the movement step to one before branching on the direction.

Select one of two direction-specific sets of four-frame poses and the mirror flag. Pass the selected frames through the resident sprite transform and store their pointers at $7FF8 plus Y as X and Y count down.
Wait ten times while alternating two groups of four frame pointers from $2D27. Restore the saved screen data to $7C00, call the resident failure display and restart the board setup.
Set the copy source to $7C00 and the destination to $0400.
Set the copy source to $0400 and the destination to $7C00. Blank the display for the four-page transfer and restore display enable afterward.
Build colour RAM from the glyph-index matrix and the lookup at $7700. Expand the glyphs into the bitmap, fill the matrix with $C2 and enable the display.
Read sequential codes from the matrix at $7C00, copy eight glyph bytes for each and stop after the bitmap write pointer reaches page $60.
Multiply the glyph code in A by eight and add $7800. Copy eight bytes through the destination pointer at $2C, advance that pointer and set carry if it is at or above $6000. Restore Y.
Copy of the Ramps state and hit sprites at $292B–$2936, including the five VIC pointers and initial frame divider.
Board pose selection, direction and the quartet toggle used by the failure animation.
Four sprite pointers read at $2A7B and $2A8E for the idle pose.
Four sprite pointers read at $2A68 and $2AA1 for the other idle pose.
Two four-pointer groups for VIC frames $80–$87, immediately ahead of the player-pose pointer tables.
Two four-pointer groups for one direction family. $2B93 and $2BA6 install pointers from this table with opposite mirror flags.
Two four-pointer groups for the other direction family. The mirror flag selects between the handling at $2B80 and $2BB9.
Two groups of four VIC pointers copied to $7FF8–$7FFB while the failure animation toggles bit 2 of $2D06.
The initializer at $1E9E writes one here. The following bytes are a separate record.
Set to one at the start and end of the movement sequence and decremented by $29F5.
Frame index written by the quartet toggle and used to choose failure poses in $2BE1.
A displacement added to or subtracted from player X by the helpers at $2AB4 and $2AD4.
Zero slot between the live horizontal movement amount and the jump offset array. The indexed jump read starts at $2D71.
Thirteen signed vertical values for the jump motion. The movement path reads the value indexed by the jump step and subtracts it from the sprite coordinate.
Frame counter incremented by $1F8E and compared with 13.
Displacement flag read by the four directional paths and cleared when a move is rolled back.
Tested at the end of the jump sequence to decide whether to show the failure poses and restart.
Copy of the Ramps bytes at $29B3–$29C4. Three zero bytes precede the fifteen codes accepted by the Ramps surface test.
Six sprite 0 pointers in the first transition family selected by the direction at $2852.
Six companion sprite 4 pointers for the same transition, loaded at $288F or $28B9.
Seven pairs of values copied by the transition handling into $2DCA/$2DCB before calling the coordinate updater.
Seven corresponding pairs for the alternate direction family.
Seven sprite 0 pointers for the alternate transition, loaded at $286E or $28EC.
Seven sprite 4 pointers from the alternate transition group.
Previous mirror setting for the transition setup and two displacement bytes taken from the direction-specific tables.
The transition completion path at $2835 clears this byte and the board update tests it at $1F27.
The transition animator increments this byte at $2828 and uses the previous value for its frame table lookup.
Four frame pointers prepared by $2933 and rearranged when copied to the primary sprite pointer slots.
The board initialization writes the first byte and fills the second from the value at $2DDD.
First nine entries of the ten-byte Ramps timer-preset record at $2A06, with four initial values shortened from $10 to $0F. The final byte at $2DDD also seeds the Phantom Knight board state.
Default byte for the saved board state at $2DD3, copied during initialization.
Copy of the Ramps hazard state at $2A10–$2A2A. It holds counters, direction and frame indices, sprite pointers, position presets and an initial collision sample.
The raster handler copies the VIC sprite collision latch here at $2C05.
The board initialization chooses this value using the shared state byte $24.
Three authored zero bytes between the initial transition selector and the cell-type table used by the board probes. The type lookup at $27B4 starts at $2DFE.
Ten rows with ten values per row. The cell queries multiply the row by ten and add the column to read a board cell type.
The target controller at $23F2 returns early when this byte is zero.
The target column and row. Both are updated by the controller and used to index the board cell type table.
Target X low, X high and Y bytes used by the board-cell address calculation and overlay sprite setup.
Direction selected by the target controller. The movement routine at $246D branches on this value.
Low X, high X and Y origin values used in the board cell conversion at $2191.
Primary and secondary countdowns used by the target movement controller at $23F2.
The target movement divider at $2E6C reloads from this byte.
Values used by the target controller when it changes the countdown presets.
After decrement this byte selects between continued movement and the alternate target-axis decision.
The player column and row, incremented or decremented by the four jump paths.
Eight saved bitmap address pairs shifted by two bytes when the target effect changes.
The next address pair read independently by the history update and checked against retained entries.
Nine initial marker bytes of value 1 before the nine saved coordinate pairs at $2E8F. The updater at $2605 shifts the markers toward the tail before inserting the newest cell type at $2613.
Nine pairs of saved board coordinates for the target history. The reward check at $2153 compares the recorded cells with the player cell.
Cell type read from $2DFE and saved for the target and bitmap drawing routines.
The callers at $25B0 and $265E select $80 or $40 here for the recolour operation at $2705.
The selected board column and row used by the proximity check and earlier effect routines.
Cell column and row copied here before the board-to-sprite-coordinate conversion at $2191.
Countdown at the head of the target-axis routine. It is reloaded with five when drawing the next effect.
Zero slot immediately after the axis decision delay at $2EAB. The countdown at $24E8 decrements $2EAB itself.
Initialized at $1E70. The reward path can increment it, and the effect routine copies it to the colour counter at $2EAF.
The effect routine copies the duration from $2EAD. The update at $23C3 decrements it while sprites 6 and 7 use the effect colour.
Cleared in the scene setup, decremented in the effect path and tested before the sprite dissolve at $2849.
The target selection path decrements this byte before drawing and clears it afterward. It is tested when choosing random effect parameters.
This scene record ends with the eleven byte marker copied by the unpacker at $0DDE.
The first $400 bytes of the character-cell-ordered board bitmap at $4000. Each cell occupies eight bytes.
Board bitmap cell bytes at offsets $0400–$07FF, in the region selected by the clear bitmap-base bit of $D018.
Pixels in board bitmap cells 256 through 383. The VIC combines them with the colours at $7C00 and in colour RAM.
Board bitmap cells 384 through 511, stored starting at $4C00 in the active VIC bank.
Bitmap cells 512 through 639. The bitmap rows use 40 such eight-byte cells.
Pixels for board bitmap cells 640 through 767. Two bits select each multicolour pixel.
Board bitmap cells 768 through 895, in the bottom part of the screen.
The final 104 board bitmap cells. The bitmap ends at $5F3F after 1000 cells.
The 24 offscreen bitmap cells generated as $2CC5 walks the entire $7C00 matrix. This output starts blank in the scene image.
Four 64-byte pose records matching the first four records at $6000 in the Ramps scene. They are the first quartet in the pointer tables used by the player sprite installer.
Four 64-byte image slots selected by sprites 0–3 in the board play capture, with pointers $84 to $87.
Two consecutive sprite masks copied to $6D00–$6D7F by $230E, selected by the first branch of the knight pose selector.
Alternative pair of sprite masks copied into the same sprite slots by $231B.
Sixteen 64-byte pose records. This part of the bitmap bank matches the same pose records in The Ramps.
Twelve sprite fragments for later player poses. The bytes of these slots match the ramp scene records.
Ten sprite frames $A8–$B1. Directions 1 and 2 select $A8 as the starting frame in the four-sprite initializer, and the transition selector uses frames through $B1.
The 64-byte image selected by sprite 5 at the Phantom Knight play capture.
Sprite pointer $B3 in VIC bank $4000 addresses this 64-byte blank frame. It sits immediately before the writable pair at $6D00.
Two 64-byte image slots selected by sprites 6 and 7 in the Phantom Knight play capture.
Five sprite frames $B6–$BA selected from the companion table at $2D99 during the transition.
Sprite pointer $BB in VIC bank $4000 addresses this 64-byte blank frame between the transition companions and the upper pose bank.
The upper bank of player fragments, with several blank slots around the start and visible limb masks in its later records. This range matches the ramp asset bank.
Eight high sprite slots with additional movement and weapon silhouettes, byte-for-byte equal to the corresponding ramp shapes.
The unpacked picture stream initializes $7500–$76FF to zero. These bytes are still zero in the play capture.
Lookup table for the colour RAM setup at $2C6B. The routine indexes it by a cell code in the initial $7C00 matrix, substitutes 6 for $0E and 1 for 9.
128 eight-byte glyphs for the initial board. The bitmap initializer at $2CC5 multiplies a matrix character code by eight and copies that glyph to the next bitmap cell.

Initial matrix of board glyph indices used by the colour and bitmap setup. Once the bitmap has been composed, the routine fills this VIC matrix with $C2. The final eight bytes then serve as sprite pointers.
The LG bytes at $A374–$A374 follow the last source token required by the scene picture decoder and precede the repeated disk fill.
Repeated $08 bytes at $A375–$A40F, after the input consumed by the scene picture decode.
